summary: A country in northeastern South America that was once a Dutch colony and became independent in 1975; it is the only country in South America with Dutch as its official language, and its ethnic groups and religions are extremely diverse.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Suriname was under Dutch rule from the 1667 Treaty of Breda (the Dutch exchanged New Amsterdam for it), and the Dutch Reformed Church was the church of the colonial elite. From 1735 German Moravian Church missionaries went deep into the plantations to preach to African slaves and their descendants, so today's Afro-Surinamese Creoles and some Maroons mostly belong to Protestant denominations such as the Moravian Church. In recent years Pentecostalism has also expanded rapidly in the cities.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: After abolition in 1863 (the transition period ended in 1873), the plantations lacked labor, and the Netherlands and Britain agreed to recruit indentured laborers from British India; the first labor ship, the Lalla Rookh, arrived in 1873, and by 1916 about 34,000 Indians had come to Suriname. Most came from Bihar and Uttar Pradesh and brought Hinduism with them; their descendants today make up more than 20 percent of the population and have formed religious organizations such as the Sanatan Dharm and the Arya Samaj.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: From the 19th century Catholicism was systematically introduced by Dutch missionaries; the famous Father Peerke Donders served at a leper colony until his death in 1887 and was later beatified by the Catholic Church. Catholic schools and medical institutions attracted conversions among Creoles, Chinese and some indigenous people, bringing the Catholic and Protestant shares roughly level.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam came mainly with two groups of indentured laborers: Hindustani Muslims from British India, and some 33,000 Javanese recruited from the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia) between 1890 and 1939. The Javanese Muslims kept their homeland custom of praying toward the west, and a dispute arose between the "Westerners" and the "Easterners" who turned toward Mecca in the east, a religious phenomenon unique to Suriname.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Those with no religion are mostly young people and the highly educated in the capital, Paramaribo, influenced by the high degree of secularization in the former colonial power, the Netherlands. Many Surinamese families have members who have moved to the Netherlands and contact between the two is frequent, so secular ideas have also come back to Suriname, but the overall share is still far lower than in the Netherlands.

ranking.name: Other (Winti, etc.)
ranking.description: Winti is a religion that formed after African slaves brought West and Central African spirit beliefs, ancestor veneration and divination rituals to Suriname, communicating with the spirits through possession and dance. The Dutch colonial government banned Winti rituals by law for a long time, until the ban was repealed in 1971, so in the past many believers could practice only in secret, and it often still coexists with Christian belief.

religion.background: Suriname's religious landscape is almost a history of migration: the Dutch colonists brought Protestantism, and African slaves brought Winti and, from the 18th century, accepted the missions of the Moravian Church. After abolition in 1863, indentured laborers from British India brought Hinduism and Islam, Javanese laborers from the Dutch East Indies added to Islam, and Chinese immigrants brought Buddhism and folk beliefs. The religions coexist in a small country, and in the capital, Paramaribo, a mosque and a synagogue stand side by side, often regarded as a symbol of religious harmony.

ranking.name: Dutch
ranking.description: Dutch became the language of administration and education when Dutch rule began in 1667, and it was kept as the sole official language after independence in 1975 because it is the shared school language of all ethnic groups and also eases contact with the large immigrant community in the Netherlands. In 2004 Suriname joined the Dutch Language Union, and it is the largest Dutch-speaking country in the Americas; about half of the people speak Dutch at home, and the rest use it at school and at work.

ranking.name: Sranan Tongo (Surinamese)
ranking.description: Sranan Tongo developed on the basis of English among African slaves on the plantations during the brief period of British rule in the 17th century, and after the Dutch took over it absorbed a great deal of Dutch and Portuguese vocabulary. It was long regarded by the colonizers as a "lowly language," but because it can bridge communication among Afro-Surinamese, Indo-Surinamese, Javanese and other groups, it became the most widely used lingua franca in the country, and many people use it as a second language.

ranking.name: Sarnami (Surinamese Hindustani)
ranking.description: Sarnami derives from the Bhojpuri and Awadhi spoken by the Indian indentured laborers who arrived in Suriname after 1873; blended locally, it formed the distinctive "Surinamese Hindustani," which also absorbed Dutch and Sranan vocabulary. It is used mainly in Indo-Surinamese homes and communities and is kept alive through Hindu temples, Bollywood films and radio.

language.history: The indigenous peoples of Suriname speak Carib and Arawak languages. In the 17th century the English and then the Dutch colonized the country; African slaves on the plantations developed the English-based Sranan Tongo, while the Maroons who fled into the interior rainforest formed languages such as Saramaccan and Ndyuka. From 1873 Indian and Javanese indentured laborers brought Sarnami and Javanese, and Chinese immigrants brought Hakka. Dutch, as the official and educational language, coexists with these languages to this day, making Suriname one of the most linguistically diverse small countries in the world.

ranking.name: Pom
ranking.description: Grated tayer (an aroid root vegetable) is layered with marinated chicken, onion and citrus juice and baked, golden on top and moist and creamy inside.
ranking.history: Pom is generally believed to derive from the Sephardic Jews who came to Suriname in the 17th century and established the "Jodensavanne" (Jewish Savanna) plantation community in the interior. Traditional Jewish dishes were originally made with potatoes, but these were hard to obtain in the tropics, so the local tayer was used instead, and later Afro-Surinamese Creoles added their own tastes. Today pom is a must at Surinamese birthday parties and holidays, and Surinamese immigrant communities in the Netherlands even put it in bread, making the very popular "pom sandwich."

ranking.name: Roti
ranking.description: A soft Indian-style flatbread served with chicken curry, potato, long beans and pickled chili, torn off and wrapped around the filling to eat.
ranking.history: Roti was brought by the Indian indentured laborers who arrived in Suriname after 1873; originally a North Indian everyday flatbread, it became, together with curry, a staple of the workers in plantation life. The Surinamese version often has ground yellow split peas inside the bread, called "dalpuri roti." With the mass emigration of Surinamese to the Netherlands in the 1970s, roti shops opened all over Amsterdam and Rotterdam and became one of the Surinamese foods best known to the Dutch.

ranking.name: Pindasoep (peanut soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup simmered for a long time with peanut butter, chicken and chili, rich and mildly spicy, often eaten with "tom tom" dumplings made of mashed cooking bananas.
ranking.history: The peanut is native to South America; in the 16th century the Portuguese brought it to Africa, where it became a major West African crop, and African slaves later brought the way of stewing peanut soup back to the Americas. In Suriname it is a signature dish of the Afro-Surinamese Creoles, and the making of "tom tom" dumplings is also close to fufu, the West African pounded starchy dumpling. Peanut soup is often made on weekends or at family gatherings and is an important symbol of Creole food culture.

ranking.name: Bami (Javanese fried noodles)
ranking.description: Egg noodles stir-fried over high heat with chicken, cabbage, bean sprouts and sweet soy sauce, savory with a touch of sweetness, often served with chili sauce, a fried egg or pickled cucumber.
ranking.history: The name "bami" derives from the Hokkien "bakmi" (meat noodles), which spread from Chinese immigrants to Indonesia and became popular in Java. Between 1890 and 1939 the Dutch recruited Javanese indentured laborers from the Dutch East Indies to Suriname, who brought Javanese-style fried noodles with them, while Chinese immigrants arriving from 1853 also ran restaurants that promoted similar noodle dishes. Today at the Javanese snack stalls in Suriname called "warungs," bami is the most popular inexpensive dish.

ranking.name: Saoto soup
ranking.description: A chicken-broth soup with shredded chicken, bean sprouts, boiled egg and fried potato or rice, topped with chili sauce, with a fragrant broth scented with lemongrass and garlic.
ranking.history: Saoto soup derives from the Indonesian "soto," brought by the Javanese indentured laborers who arrived in Suriname after 1890, and its spelling was adapted to local Dutch habits. It was originally an everyday Javanese soup that later became very popular among all of Suriname's ethnic groups and is often eaten as a weekend brunch or a hangover soup. It is also widely served in Surinamese and Javanese restaurants in the Netherlands and is one of the representative dishes of Suriname's diverse immigrant cuisine.
